reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Defined as sudden, brief, shock-like involuntary movements, which may be positive (muscle contraction) or negative (a lapse of tone, as in asterixis)
Classified clinically by distribution (focal, segmental, multifocal, or generalised) and by trigger, such as action or stimulus-sensitive myoclonus
Aetiologically grouped into physiological, essential, epileptic, and symptomatic (secondary) forms, the last being the most common in clinical practice
A crucial step is to identify secondary causes, particularly metabolic and toxic encephalopathies, since these are often reversible
Asterixis (negative myoclonus) is a classic sign of hepatic, renal, and other metabolic encephalopathies
Neurophysiological localisation into cortical, subcortical, spinal, or peripheral origin helps guide investigation and treatment
Post-hypoxic action myoclonus (Lance-Adams syndrome) can follow cardiac arrest and cerebral hypoxia
Treatment principles combine correcting any underlying cause with symptomatic antimyoclonic agents chosen according to the presumed generator
reference.pathophysiology: Myoclonus results from abnormal, excessive neuronal discharge that can arise at several levels of the nervous system. Cortical myoclonus reflects hyperexcitability of the sensorimotor cortex and often coexists with epilepsy; subcortical and brainstem forms arise from deeper generators; and spinal and peripheral forms originate in the cord or nerve. Loss of normal inhibitory control, frequently involving impaired GABAergic and serotonergic mechanisms, allows brief synchronous muscle discharges. Underlying processes include metabolic derangement, drugs and toxins, neurodegeneration, hypoxia, and epilepsy.
additionalInvestigations: Metabolic screen including renal, hepatic, glucose, electrolyte, and calcium studies to identify reversible causes
Review of medications and toxins that can provoke myoclonus
EEG, including back-averaging with EMG, to identify a cortical origin and epileptic activity
MRI of the brain and, where relevant, the spinal cord to seek structural or degenerative causes
Targeted testing for infective, autoimmune, paraneoplastic, or metabolic-genetic disorders when indicated
redFlags: Myoclonus with declining consciousness suggesting a serious metabolic, toxic, or hypoxic encephalopathy
Rapidly progressive myoclonus with cognitive decline raising concern for prion disease or an autoimmune encephalitis
Myoclonus following cardiac arrest, which may indicate severe hypoxic brain injury
Myoclonus as part of a status myoclonicus or in the context of status epilepticus requiring urgent treatment
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is dictated by the underlying cause. Myoclonus due to reversible metabolic or drug causes typically resolves once the trigger is corrected, whereas myoclonus from neurodegenerative, prion, or severe hypoxic injury carries a poor outlook. Symptomatic treatment can meaningfully reduce disability in many chronic cases even when the cause cannot be cured.
pitfalls: Failing to search for and correct a reversible metabolic or drug-induced cause
Misclassifying myoclonus as tremor, tics, or seizures and mismanaging it
Overlooking a serious progressive cause such as prion disease or autoimmune encephalitis
Not localising the myoclonus neurophysiologically, leading to poorly targeted therapy
management: Identify and correct the underlying cause, especially reversible metabolic derangements and offending drugs or toxins
Localise the generator neurophysiologically as cortical, subcortical, spinal or peripheral to guide drug selection
Treat cortical myoclonus with antiseizure agents such as levetiracetam, sodium valproate or clonazepam
Manage myoclonus of other origins with clonazepam alongside cause-directed therapy
Manage acute severe myoclonus, including post-hypoxic status myoclonus, with escalating antiseizure and anaesthetic therapy and supportive care
Investigate for structural, autoimmune, paraneoplastic or neurodegenerative causes and refer to neurology
